children: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's first rate decision is putting his policy approach and credibility under scrutiny, with markets watching not just the size of the move but also what it signals about the path ahead.

The market had harbored doubts about Warsh's personal credibility even before he took the Fed chair, and that may have contributed to what Dario Perkins, managing director of global macro at TS Lombard, described as "virtue signaling," he said in a post on X on Wednesday. Perkins added that the Fed may have reached a “moment of truth.”

In a note, Steven Blitz, economist at TS Lombard, said Warsh would raise rates by 25 basis points but argued that he “should hike 50” based even on his policy playbook. Blitz said Warsh's decision not to make a larger move was a signal that he still believed in the real growth and disinflation story or that he understood rising longer-term yields could do more work than raising the federal funds rate.

Blitz also said the move would not necessarily mark the start of a smooth tightening cycle, warning that markets should prepare for a “bumpy ride.” He said rising real-term yields could weigh on equities more than higher short-term rates and argued that the route to slowing the economy could run through risk assets and household balance sheets.

The note pointed to the growing importance of equities in household wealth. Blitz said the share of household net worth represented by equities had reached post-war records, making household wealth more vulnerable to an equity-market reversal. He argued that higher bond yields would eventually need to offer more competitive returns relative to equities.

Perkins' comments and Blitz's analysis put the focus on a broader question surrounding Warsh's tenure: whether his policy choices and communication can establish credibility with markets while navigating an economy in which longer-term yields are playing an increasingly important role.
The comments come as the Federal Open Market Committee is widely expected to raise its benchmark rate to 3.75%-4.00% from the current target range of 3.50%-3.75% at its September meeting.

If effective, the hike will be the Fed's first since July 2023 but unlikely to be the last for this year. A September hike could be the first in a cycle of monetary policy tightening, according to a report by S&P Global Market Intelligence.
This week's meeting is Kevin Warsh's third heading the central bank.
Warsh has staunchly defended his view that the so-called “forward guidance”, or signalling the likely direction of the FOMC's policy path, isn't useful.

So, the FOMC statement will likely only provide commentary on the current decision rather than insight into where rates are heading. Therefore, the Summary of Economic Projections, particularly the closely watched “dot plot”, will be of significance.

title: Warsh faces credibility test as Fed decision looms, TS Lombard's Perkins says
